c.entradas.ninhursag.nombre_original: Nin-hursaĝa (Sumerian, 'Lady of the mountain'); also Ninmah, Nintu, Belet-ili, Mami
c.entradas.ninhursag.fecha_texto: Attested from the Early Dynastic period.
c.entradas.ninhursag.resumen: Mother goddess and goddess of childbirth. She takes part in the creation of human beings. Under several names (Ninmah, Nintu, Mami, Belet-ili) she is considered the midwife of gods and humans.
c.entradas.ninhursag.interpretacion:
Black and Green note that the mother goddesses of Mesopotamia gradually merged into a single figure with many names. Her importance in the god lists of the 3rd millennium, sometimes alongside An, Enlil and Enki, declined over time. Lugal-e explains the name Ninhursag as a title given by her son Ninurta.

Her symbol may be an omega-shaped sign (Ω), interpreted as a uterus or a birthing instrument, although the identification is debated.
c.entradas.ninhursag.detalles.0: Her cult centers were Kesh and Adab.
c.entradas.ninhursag.detalles.1: In Atrahasis, as Nintu/Mami, she shapes the first humans.
c.entradas.ninhursag.detalles.2: In 'Enki and Ninhursag' she curses and then heals Enki.
c.entradas.ninhursag.detalles.3: Some Early Dynastic kings claimed to be 'nourished with the milk' of Ninhursag.
c.entradas.ninhursag.fuentes_primarias.0: Temple of Ninhursag at Tell al-'Ubaid (reliefs in the British Museum)
c.entradas.utu-shamash.fecha_texto: Attested from the 3rd millennium BC and worshiped until late times.
c.entradas.utu-shamash.resumen: God of the sun, justice and divination. He sees everything that happens on earth and judges the living and the dead. His cities were Sippar and Larsa.
c.entradas.utu-shamash.interpretacion:
Because the sun sees everything, he is the guarantor of oaths and of justice. That is why he presides over the stele of the Code of Hammurabi, where he hands the king the insignia of power. Together with Adad, he is also patron of extispicy, divination by the entrails of animals.

In iconography he usually carries a toothed saw and appears rising between mountains. His symbol is a disk with a four-pointed star and wavy rays between its points. In Assyria he is sometimes associated with the winged disk, although that identification is a matter of debate.
c.entradas.utu-shamash.detalles.0: His main temple is the Ebabbar ('white/shining house') at Sippar and at Larsa.
c.entradas.utu-shamash.detalles.1: The stele of Hammurabi (Louvre, c. 1750 BC) shows him enthroned.
c.entradas.utu-shamash.detalles.2: The Sun God Tablet of Sippar (British Museum, 9th century BC) depicts his solar disk.
c.entradas.utu-shamash.detalles.3: His sacred number is 20 and his wife is Aya.
c.entradas.utu-shamash.fuentes_primarias: Stele of the Code of Hammurabi (Louvre)
Sun God Tablet of Sippar (British Museum)
c.entradas.nanna-sin.fecha_texto: Attested from the 3rd millennium BC. His cult at Harran remained alive in late antiquity.
c.entradas.nanna-sin.resumen: God of the moon and patron of the city of Ur. He measured time with his phases and was the father of Utu and Inanna. His great ziggurat at Ur has been partly preserved.
c.entradas.nanna-sin.interpretacion:
The Mesopotamian calendar was lunar, hence Nanna's importance. The kings of Akkad and Ur III appointed their daughters as his priestesses, such as Enheduanna, daughter of Sargon and priestess at Ur. In this way the cult underpinned dynastic legitimacy.

The Neo-Babylonian king Nabonidus (556–539 BC) promoted him to an exceptional degree, especially at Harran. According to later propaganda texts, this devotion set the king against the clergy of Marduk in Babylon.
c.entradas.nanna-sin.detalles.0: His temple is the Ekishnugal at Ur, and his ziggurat was built by Ur-Nammu, c. 2100 BC.
c.entradas.nanna-sin.detalles.1: His symbol is the crescent moon and his sacred number is 30.
c.entradas.nanna-sin.detalles.3: Nabonidus restored his Ehulhul temple at Harran.
c.entradas.nanna-sin.fuentes_primarias.0: Ziggurat of Ur (excavations by Leonard Woolley)
c.entradas.marduk.nombre_original: Marduk (Akkadian; written AMAR.UTU, perhaps 'bull calf of Utu'); also called Bēl, 'Lord'
c.entradas.marduk.fecha_texto: Local god of Babylon from the 3rd millennium BC. He rose with Hammurabi (18th century BC) and became head of the Babylonian pantheon toward the end of the 2nd millennium BC.
c.entradas.marduk.resumen: God of the city of Babylon. Along with the city's political power, he became king of the gods. In the Enuma Elish he defeats Tiamat and orders the cosmos.
c.entradas.marduk.interpretacion:
Marduk's history shows how Mesopotamian theology reflected politics. The god of a minor city gained importance as Babylon became a capital. The return of his statue from Elam under Nebuchadnezzar I is considered a key moment in his theological exaltation. The Enuma Elish transfers Enlil's functions to him, and late texts describe other gods as 'aspects' of Marduk, something some scholars regard as a henotheistic tendency.

In the sky, his star was Jupiter, which in certain positions was called Nēberu. His animal is the mušhuššu, a serpent-dragon, and his symbol is the triangular spade (marru).
c.entradas.marduk.detalles.0: His temple is the Esagila in Babylon and his ziggurat is the Etemenanki.
c.entradas.marduk.detalles.1: His symbol is the triangular spade (marru) and his animal is the mušhuššu dragon.
c.entradas.marduk.detalles.2: He is the son of Ea (Enki), and his son is Nabu, god of writing.
c.entradas.marduk.detalles.3: His statue was carried off to Elam, Assyria and Persia at different times, and its return was a political event.
c.entradas.marduk.detalles.4: His planet is Jupiter, called Nēberu in certain positions.
c.entradas.marduk.fuentes_primarias.1: Excavations of the Esagila and the Etemenanki, Babylon
c.entradas.marduk.fuentes_primarias.2: Kassite kudurrus with the spade symbol
c.entradas.ashur.nombre_original: Aššur (Akkadian); the city and the god share the name
c.entradas.ashur.fecha_texto: God of the city of Assur from the early 2nd millennium BC or earlier. He was the national god of the Assyrian empire until its fall in 612–609 BC.
c.entradas.ashur.resumen: Supreme god of Assyria, identified with his city. The Assyrian king was his vicar and priest. Ashur granted victory and the expansion of the empire.
c.entradas.ashur.interpretacion:
Ashur is a unique case: originally he seems to be the deification of a place, perhaps the city's promontory. That is why he has no ancient mythology of his own. Over time he was identified with Enlil and, in the time of Sennacherib, with Anshar, the primordial ancestor in the Enuma Elish, in order to place him above Marduk. The Assyrian versions of the poem replace Marduk with Ashur.

Assyrian royal ideology presented military campaigns as a mandate from Ashur. The winged disk with a human figure is traditionally attributed to him, although Black and Green caution that this identification is not certain and that the symbol might represent Shamash.
c.entradas.ashur.detalles.0: His temple is the Esharra, at Assur (Qal'at Sherqat).
c.entradas.ashur.detalles.1: The Assyrian king bore the title 'vicar (iššiakku) of Ashur'.
c.entradas.ashur.detalles.2: Sennacherib reformed the New Year festival at Assur, putting Ashur in Marduk's place.
c.entradas.ashur.detalles.3: It is debated whether the winged disk on Assyrian reliefs represents Ashur or Shamash.
c.entradas.ashur.fuentes_primarias.0: Excavations at Assur (Walter Andrae, Deutsche Orient-Gesellschaft)
c.entradas.ashur.fuentes_primarias.2: Assyrian version of the Enuma Elish
replaces Marduk in the Assyrian version of
c.entradas.ereshkigal.nombre_original: Ereš-ki-gal (Sumerian, 'Lady of the great earth', that is, of the Underworld)
c.entradas.ereshkigal.fecha_texto: Attested from the 3rd millennium BC. She is a protagonist of Old Babylonian myths and of myths from the 2nd–1st millennia BC.
c.entradas.ereshkigal.resumen: Queen of the Underworld and elder sister of Inanna. She rules from her palace in the land of no return, with the help of her vizier Namtar. Later she is presented as the wife of Nergal.
c.entradas.ereshkigal.interpretacion:
Ereshkigal represents the unchangeable order of death. Not even Inanna can escape it. The myths show her as both fearsome and vulnerable: she weeps for her children or for the lover who leaves.

Her pairing with Nergal seems secondary and explains the fusion of two traditions. In iconography she has no secure type, and the famous 'Burney Relief' (Queen of the Night, British Museum) has been identified with her, with Inanna or with Lilith, with no consensus.
c.entradas.ereshkigal.detalles.1: Her first husband is Gugalanna, according to the Descent of Inanna.
c.entradas.ereshkigal.detalles.2: In the Underworld, the Anunnaki accompany her as judges.
c.entradas.ereshkigal.detalles.3: The identification of the 'Burney Relief' (British Museum, c. 1750 BC) is disputed.
c.entradas.nergal.nombre_original: Nergal (Sumerian, probably 'Lord of the great city', that is, of the Underworld); identified with Erra
c.entradas.nergal.fecha_texto: Attested from the 3rd millennium BC; his cult at Kutha was already documented in the Akkadian period.
c.entradas.nergal.resumen: God of war, plague and sudden death, and king of the Underworld alongside Ereshkigal. His city was Kutha. He was identified with Erra.
c.entradas.nergal.interpretacion:
Nergal combines the violence of the scorching summer sun, war and epidemic. That is why he was invoked both to cause harm and for protection against it. His relationship with Erra allows the Poem of Erra and Ishum to be read in terms of plague and destruction.

In astronomy he is associated with the planet Mars, reddish in color and considered ill-omened. His symbol is a mace with lion heads.
c.entradas.nergal.detalles.0: His temple is the Emeslam at Kutha.
c.entradas.nergal.detalles.2: His symbol is the lion-headed mace or scepter.
c.entradas.nergal.detalles.3: The Bible (2 Kings 17:30) mentions 'the men of Cuth' who made an image of Nergal.
c.entradas.tiamat.fecha_texto: Mainly in the Enuma Elish (late 2nd millennium BC). The term 'sea' as a cosmic force is older.
c.entradas.tiamat.resumen: Personification of the sea, of the primordial salt waters. With Apsu she begets the first gods. When Apsu dies, she creates an army of monsters and is finally defeated by Marduk, who forms the universe from her body.
c.entradas.tiamat.interpretacion:
Tiamat represents the primordial watery chaos, but in the Enuma Elish she is not just a monster. At first she is a patient mother who defends her children, and only later does she become hostile. The popular image of Tiamat as a dragon does not appear in the text, which is ambiguous about her form.

Scholars connect Marduk's battle against Tiamat with the motif of the 'storm god versus the sea', also present at Ugarit (Baal versus Yam) and in some biblical passages. Since Hermann Gunkel (1895) it has been compared with the tehom of Genesis, although today that relationship is understood as a kinship of motifs and vocabulary, not as direct borrowing.
c.entradas.tiamat.detalles.0: Her name derives from Akkadian tâmtu, 'sea'.
c.entradas.tiamat.detalles.1: She creates eleven monsters, among them the mušhuššu and the scorpion-man.
c.entradas.tiamat.detalles.2: Marduk splits her in two: with one half he makes the sky and with the other the earth. The Tigris and the Euphrates spring from her eyes.
c.entradas.tiamat.detalles.3: Her second consort is Qingu, to whom she gives the Tablet of Destinies.
c.entradas.tiamat.fuentes_primarias.0: Enuma Elish (tablets from Assur, Nineveh and Babylon)
c.entradas.apsu.fecha_texto: The cosmic concept is attested from the 3rd millennium BC. It appears personified as a god in the Enuma Elish (late 2nd millennium BC).
c.entradas.apsu.resumen: In Mesopotamian cosmology, the Apsu is the ocean of fresh water beneath the earth, from which springs and rivers flow. It is the domain of Enki/Ea. In the Enuma Elish it appears personified as the primordial father, whom Ea kills.
c.entradas.apsu.interpretacion:
In the Sumerian tradition, the abzu is above all a place, the underground realm of Enki, and his temple at Eridu was called E-abzu. In temples, a pool or basin of purified water was also called 'apsû'.

The Enuma Elish personifies it as a god who, annoyed by the noise of the young gods, wants to destroy them. Ea puts him to sleep with an incantation, kills him and builds his dwelling on top of him. In this way the poem explains why the underground water is Ea's home.
c.entradas.apsu.detalles.0: Enki's temple at Eridu was called E-abzu, 'house of the abzu'.
c.entradas.apsu.detalles.1: Some temples had ritual basins called 'apsû'.
c.entradas.apsu.detalles.2: In the Enuma Elish, Apsu's vizier is Mummu.
c.entradas.apsu.detalles.3: The motif of the 'noise' that disturbs the primordial god also appears in Atrahasis.
